verdicts.trueWording: without actually knowing what's in the Fiend Folio
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200) post #67 by Hemlock: 'They all exist in the 5E MMs though. A good illustration of the limits of GPT: apparently it's aware that these monsters tend to be discussed adjacent to the Fiend Folio, without actually knowing what's in the Fiend Folio.' The first limb is carried by Beoric's quoted post on the same page: 'It is worth mentioning that as far as I can tell some of those monsters do not appear in any version of the FF that I am aware of.' The generated room listed Hezrous, Gibbering mouthers, Grell, Vargouilles and Dretch as Fiend Folio monsters. Both source statements are hedged ('as far as I can tell', 'apparently'); the claim states them flatly.

verdicts.trueWording: there were similarities with the original room
verdicts.note: Raw page, Beoric post #64: after asking for 'a unique encounter in the trick room', he writes 'The other is that there were similarities with the original room; I assume this is because it has a limited data set of D&D adventures to draw on. I suspect that if you use it a lot, you would have to seed it with your own elements.' Both limbs supported. Minor softening: the page says 'I suspect ... if you use it a lot', the claim says 'concluded'.

verdicts.trueWording: motivated by greed and loyalty to their goblin boss
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, so graded on substance. Raw page 1 of the thread carries Beoric's transcript. The phrase 'They are motivated by greed and loyalty to their goblin boss' recurs verbatim across at least six entries (lighthouse basement, dungeon entrance, guard room, armory, kitchen, treasure room) — the claim's parenthetical drops the word 'goblin'. Every creature entry follows one identical block ('They are not initially hostile, but will attack if provoked ... They are motivated by ... They want ... They have a fear of ... They are currently ...'). 'Guard room' entry 3 recurs on dungeon level 1 and again on level 2 in near-identical wording. Two caveats a reader should see: that block format was dictated by Beoric's own prompt, and the village NPC list earlier in the transcript uses a different (also prompt-dictated) template, so 'every NPC in the same template' holds within a key, not across the whole transcript.

verdicts.trueWording: They offer the illusion of help
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'I find LLMs useful for small coding projects but they don't help me with RPGs. They offer the illusion of help, but my best RPG work is the work I do myself.' Rendered text matches the quote word for word (the em tag is markup only). Byline 'by Mike on 30 September 2024'; site footer names Michael E. Shea. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: They fill the internet with slop.
verdicts.note:
Raw HTML: '
  • They fill the internet with slop.
    • ' — rendered visible text is the quote exactly. It is the fourth of four bulleted costs, the others being 'built on people's intellectual property without their permission and without compensation', 'They use tons of power and water', and 'They displace workers with shitty AI alternatives' — i.e. the IP, energy and labour objections the claim names. The subject on the page is generative AI tools generally, not 'LLM output' narrowly.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the bar generated boxed text is measured against by reviewers
verdicts.trueWording: Keep it short and keep it powerful.
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim on the raw page. The craft limbs all check out: 'Know the purpose of your read-aloud text up front'; 'If you didn't edit your read-aloud text and remove 25% of what was there, you didn't try hard enough.' Byline 'by Mike on 8 November 2010' matches. But the page is a 2010 article that never mentions generated text, AI, or reviewers measuring machine output against this standard — that final limb is the researcher's framing, not on the page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the opposite of the padded, withholding generated style
verdicts.trueWording: Players understand about half of what we describe to them.
verdicts.note: No quote supplied. Raw page ('Tell, Don't Show', by Mike on 12 February 2024) supports the reported limbs: 'Players understand about half of what we describe to them.'; a section 'Don't Hold Your Cards Too Close' against DMs holding back information; and 'Feel free to keep your language colorful and stay in the world but state clearly what the characters know, or should know, about the situation.' The withholding it criticises is the human GM's, not a model's — the page says nothing about generated prose, so the closing comparison is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: a human writer who just needs a lot of editing
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'The fast iteration, though, is much more like interact with a human writer who just needs a lot of editing.' (sic, page's own grammar). Second limb also on the page: 'if the GPT produces something I almost like, but not quite, I can keep the bit I did like and use it as a prompt again, perhaps with a new random seed.' Title confirms 'The Uncanny Deck: Co-authoring with GPT-2'.

verdicts.trueWording: takes more training data to tune it to remember deeper associations
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'But it takes more training data to tune it to remember deeper associations and themes — like “salt is associated with archiving” or “venom is associated with drugs and bright colours.”' The contrast with surface form is the preceding sentence: 'I could fairly easily train a GPT model to create outputs that structurally resembled the card-description pattern I had'. Only overstatement is the intensifier 'far more'; the page says 'more'.

verdicts.trueWording: spontaneously pop up a combo of rank and suit
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'But sometimes it will spontaneously pop up a combo of rank and suit that don't exist in the original — just as I hoped from the fantasy version of the deck. “Ghost” is a rank in the original corpus, but “Butterflock” is not a suit there'. 'Absent from the corpus' and 'welcome for the fantasy deck' both supported. 'Outside the intended parameters' reads correctly only as outside the original grammar/corpus — the page elsewhere says the model strays 'from the constraints of the original grammar' and 'gets further from what the model was trained to do'; for this specific case the author wanted it.

verdicts.trueWording: it would produce boring, robotic answers
verdicts.note: Raw page, Data Scientist Melanie Lopez Malet: 'if you were to talk to a basic language model, it would produce boring, robotic answers. By conditioning the statistics within the model to go in the direction you want, based on the backstory, personality, and dialogue style as envisioned by a writer, it begins to understand what you expect.' Both limbs supported; article dated March 19, 2024, by Lucy O'Brien.

Raw page: 'while we're talking to it, we ask ourselves: “is this Lisa? Would Lisa say this?” and if the answer is no, we need to go back and find out what happened within the model to make it stray from the vision Virginie had.' Both limbs supported. 'Constantly' is a mild strengthening of 'while we're talking to it'.

Raw page, under 'Catching Bias': '“we created a physically attractive female character,” explains Malet, “and its answers veered towards flirtatious and seductive, so we had to reprogram it”.' Every limb supported verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a lot of content for them to be more coherent
verdicts.note: Raw page: Mosser, in a post-demo panel — 'So my role is to nurture them [NEO NPCs] to build the backstory, the flow, the qualities, the colloquialisms, because it's important for the dialogue style. It takes a lot of content for them to be more coherent, to have a real personality and a real focus for emotion'. Title 'narrative director', the four content types, coherence and real personality all present. Byline Michael Higham, March 19, 2024.

verdicts.trueWording: more structured like a traditional dialogue tree; an optimal choice existed
verdicts.note: No quote supplied. Raw page: 'The third and final phase of the demo had me planning an operation to infiltrate a building alongside a new NPC named Iron. While talking to her and asking questions provided more insight on the goals of the operation, it was more structured like a traditional dialogue tree: there were correct responses for the best outcome; for example, suggesting the team's hacker disable cameras as opposed to creating cover with smoke grenades was the optimal choice.' The steering limb is carried by the immediately following paragraph — 'the Ubisoft narrative team dictates the parameters for NEO NPCs to be compliant within the bounds of the lore and story of the experience, so there is a level of curation' — and by Inworld CEO Kylan Gibbs on 'narrative controls, making sure that you're not going outside of the intended domain of the world'. The word 'guardrails' is the researcher's, not the article's.
